debate.title:
Discussion on the Electricity Regulatory Commissions
(Amendment) Bill, 1999. (Bill passed.)

turns.label: MR. SPEAKER
turns.text:
Now, we take up item no. 13. The House has to allot time for discussion on this Bill as the time has not been allotted.

Shall we allot one hour?

turns.label: SOME HON. MEMBERS
turns.text: Yes.

turns.label: Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu
turns.text:
विद्युत मंत्री (श्री सुरेश प्रभु): अध्यक्ष महोदय, इस सदन ने रेगुलेटरी कमीशन 1998 को पारित किया था। इसके तहत कानून में ऐसे प्रावधान थे जिससे c® राज्य को रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन करना था। इसके बाद कई राज्यों ने इस तरह के रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन किया।

ऐसे कई राज्य हैं जिन्होंने अपने खुद के कानून पारित करके इस इलैक्ट्रसिटी रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन किया है। केन्p सरकार के पास ऐसे कई राज्यों के रिप्रेजेंटेशन्स आये हैं जिसमें कहा गया है कि कई ऐसे छोटे राज्य हैं जिनके लिये रैगुलेटरी कमीशन बनाना आप्रेशनली ज्यादा इफैक्टिव नहीं होगा। इसलिये, इस बात को ध्यान में रखते हुये हमने इस तरह का कानून लाने का निर्णय किया है जिसमें एक से ज्यादा छोटे राज्यों के लिये जाइंट रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन करना संभव होगा।

अध्यक्ष महोदय, आपने इस बिल को पहले स्टैंडिंग कमेटी को रैफर किया था और उसने अपनी रिकमैंडेशन्स दे दी हैं जिन्हें इस बिल में सम्मिलित करके इस बिल को सुधार करके सदन में लाये हैं। मेरी सदन से प्रार्थना है कि जिस तरह पहले इस बिल को पारित किया था, उसी तरह इस बिल को भी पारित किया जाये ताकि एक से ज्यादा छोटे राज्यो के लिये यह रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन करना सम्भव हो सके।

अध्यक्ष महोदय, मैं प्रस्ताव करता हूं:

turns.label: SHRI V.P. SINGH BADNORE (BHILWARA)
turns.text:
Sir, I rise to support the proposed Bill amending the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and the States’ Electricity Regulatory Commissions. The Electricity Regulatory Commission Bill became an Act in 1998. This Bill has a very limited role. In the Bill, there was no consideration for small States, which cannot afford to have a State Electricity Regulatory Commission because the Electricity Regulatory Commission in every State must have a lot of other things, like a building, a Commission and other paraphernalia, which is very difficult for a small State to spend so much money on it. The North-Eastern States especially do not want to spend so much money on this. That is why, this Bill is being mooted, and I support it wholeheartedly.

I think, this is also an opportunity for us to look into the working of the CERC and the SERCs. This Bill is okay. There may be small problems in this Bill, like if the five North-Eastern States want to have a common State Electricity Regulatory Commission, then who is going to be its Chairman and so on. Alternately, one of the members will have to be its Chairman. It can create some problems; it can also create small problems, like where this State Electricity Regulatory Commission is going to be housed, in which State it is going to be housed and so on. They have to decide this. If they can decide it very amiably, I think, nobody will have any problems about it. It also has only three members in it. Now, if five States are going to have three members, then they may have some problems in deciding who is going to be the member, and who is not going to be the member. This has been left to them, and they are going to sort it out through a consensus. However, I look at it on a bigger scenario.

Sir, this is the first Bill being piloted by our new Minister of Power, Shri Suresh Prabhu. I feel that he has a big problem to sort out a lot of other issues.

15.00 hrs.

Power is the biggest problem area in this country. Nothing moves without power. Though Shri Yashwant Sinha has presented a very good Budget, yet if there is no power and if there is a shortfall in power and energy, then nothing will move ahead. The IT industry would not move ahead and the other industries also would not move ahead. We would not be able to do any developmental work without power.

Sir, but I would like to congratulate the hon. Minister in a way. He has been really working hard on it. It has come to our notice from the reports of the newspapers that the hon. Minister has been trying to understand the problems of this nature. There are many problems that plague the power sector. The biggest of them is that, though the public sector units like the NTPC and NHPC have been performing well, the private sector participation in this sector has not been up to the expectations. There has been a shortfall only because the private sector has not come into this sector the way it should have.

Sir, I would not like to go into the long history as to why it has not been happening. I would also not like to go into securitisation and counter-guarantees and such other things. It is because the scope of this Bill is very limited. I would only like to talk about the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and what it has achieved during the last two and a half years. This Commission came into being in the year 1998. What we must see here is this. Has this Commission really taken off? Has it really performed? Why was this Commission set up? Why should we at all have this Commission? Is it doing its work? These are the questions on which we have to ponder over today.

15.02 hrs. (Shri P.H.Pandiyan in the Chair)

Sir, the few orders that this Commission has passed have been challenged in the Courts. They had come out with an Order regarding `availability based tariff’. I would like to talk on this subject today. This order of `availability based tariff’ has been challenged by NTPC and this would be challenged in the future also. What exactly is this `availability based tariff’ for the NTPC? The order basically seeks to increase the benchmark level on availability for generating companies from the earlier established level of 68.49 plant load factor to 80 per cent.

Sir, earlier there were some problems with TRAI in this regard. That is why, in this Act of the Regulatory Commission, there was a provision saying that the Ministry would be involved and would also be able to give directions to the Regulatory Commission so that the repetition of the problems that TRAI faced would not be there in the field of electricity as well.

I feel that the Ministry has not been concerned over this. If the Ministry has been concerned, they would have seen that orders like these are not passed. Why should an order be passed against NTPC? Tomorrow it may be passed against the NHPC also. Those are the performing public sector units and the surplus money that they are making is being ploughed back for augmentation of the power industry only. I would request that this be looked into. I feel that some sort of directions from the Ministry must go to the CERC regarding passing of such orders.

One of the reasons why the Regulatory Commissions came into being was that we wanted to have an independent body to look into the tariff structure. The SEBs have all failed today. They are all in the red because the States have not been able to pay to SEBs. If SEBs are not performing well, and if they continue to be in the red, there is going to be more problems in this industry. To look into this whole affair CERC and SERCs have been set up. I would like to know if any orders of SERCs have really gone into the tariff realisation so far. If they have failed to do this, who is going to pay this subsidy amount?

This particular Bill is a very small Bill and in this context I am talking. I would say in the bigger context that CERC and SERCs have not really performed. This is what the Minister must explain to us.

With these words, I support this Bill.

turns.label: Pawan Kumar Bansal
turns.text:
Mr. Chairman, Sir, this Bill has ostensibly been moved to meet the need and demand of smaller States to enable them to set up Joint Electricity Regulatory Commissions. This is a welcome measure.

By the way the ‘Statement of Objects and Reasons’ of the Bill has been wrongly printed as ‘Statement of Objections and Reasons’.

turns.label: Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu
turns.text: Your objection is sustained, Sir.

turns.label: Pawan Kumar Bansal
turns.text:
Thank you. That was just by the way.

The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill refers to the communication that the Government of India had received from the Government of Nagaland for constitution of a joint North-Eastern Electricity Regulatory Commission for four States – Assam, Mizoram, Manipur and Nagaland. Besides Nagaland, we are told that Sikkim and other North-Eastern States have also indicated their problems in setting up individual Commissions due to factors like paucity of funds, personnel, talent, etc. Therefore, this Bill becomes the need of the hour, if we really wish to subserve the objective of the main legislation.

Besides that, I also think that via this Bill, we could set the pace for cooperation between different States. Today, we find that the borders of the States tend to become borders of contention, I suppose, cooperation between the States in setting up of joint bodies on matters beginning with the Electricity Regulatory Commission would serve a very useful purpose, and such borders would, in fact, become places where the citizens of one State are out to meet with a smile their friends from the other States.

Sir, having said that, I would like to seize this opportunity to refer to the peculiar problem of the place I come from. We talk of small States. I come from a small Union Territory. Unfortunately, the need of the Union Territory of Chandigarh has not been taken care of the way it should have been. Many years back, we were assured of a generation plant there at Chandigarh itself. We are now told that it would not be viable and it would be a difficult proposition. Though I would wish that we have one, but I do not intend to dispute the assessment of the Government in this regard.

But, Sir, what I would really like to point out is that, for not years but for decades, we have been raising a demand for according us our due in the form of membership of Bhakra Beas Management Board. That is our legitimate right even according to the provisions of the Punjab Reorganisation Act. But somehow, it is Punjab and Haryana perhaps, the two States which have adopted a big-brotherly attitude and resisted the membership of Chandigarh to the Bhakra Beas Management Board. Despite the fact that Chandigarh has an excellent record of distribution and even resource generation on many counts, while States like Punjab -- as we have seen in the past -- have been squandering away their resources on the populous measures, yet Chandigarh has to suffer for no fault of its own. Whenever the question of fixation of tariff arises, we are told, "Well, these are the rates prevailing in the adjoining State of Punjab. Therefore, Chandigarh must have the same rate." There is no rationale behind that. But we, people of Chandigarh, are helpless.

We do not have a representative body like the Legislative Assembly where the aspirations, yearnings and the needs of the people could be articulated. We have to content with what is decided by the Government of India here and finally implemented through its officers at Chandigarh.

Sir, if the membership of BBMB is accorded to Chandigarh, Chandigarh would draw power at lesser rate.

turns.label: MR. CHAIRMAN
turns.text: Since, there is no panel of Chairmen present here, and as I have to join the Business Advisory Committee meeting in hon. Speaker’s Chamber, if the House agrees, I would request Shri G.M. Banatwalla to occupy the Chair.

turns.label: SOME HON. MEMBERS
turns.text:
Sure, Sir.

15.14 hrs (Shri G.M. Banatwalla in the Chair )

turns.label: Pawan Kumar Bansal
turns.text:
Mr. Chairman, Sir, if Chandigarh is accorded membership of Bhakra Beas Management Board, the rate at which electricity would be provided to Chandigarh would come down, with the result, people would get electricity at cheaper rate. You leave it to the Administration that it must not incur losses thereon. That is fine. But the people must not be taxed for no fault of theirs, rather, they should not be deprived of their right which is there.

In the past, we have seen that whenever the tariff of electricity in the Union Territory has been enhanced thoughtlessly, there is always a steep hike even in the minimum charges fixed. I can understand the concept of fixation of minimum charges for industry and for commercial sector.

To have minimum charges for domestic consumers and that too at an abnormally high rate is beyond imagination and without rationale. Chandigarh is a place where people have houses of an acre or even more than an acre.

turns.label: Nitish Sengupta
turns.text: But do not pay the house tax.

turns.label: Pawan Kumar Bansal
turns.text:
I will deal with the question as to why the people of Chandigarh would not pay that separately. It is because they were coaxed to come to Chandigarh. Perhaps the hon. Member is not aware of the circumstances in which the city of Chandigarh was raised. Pandit Nehru took interest in it; Sardar Pratap Singh Kairon took interest in it. They in fact promised much more than what the people there are getting today to go and settle in Chandigarh. That is how this city was then raised.

I was referring to the abnormal increase in the rates of minimum charges. People living in big houses are generally retired people. There are just two retired elderly people in those houses – the husband and the wife – with their children settled in other places. On the one hand, we exhort people to save electricity. Maybe the sanctioned load for those houses is much bigger but going by the advice of the Government and going by the need of the society to save electricity, they would switch off the light when they go out and switch on the fan when they come back. That way, they save electricity wherever possible. But they often find that the charges that are slapped on them are much more than what they have actually consumed. Is that fair in such cases? I would take this opportunity to impress upon the hon. Minister to ensure that as far as the domestic consumers are concerned such burden should not be imposed on them and the bills should be just according to the actual consumption of the residents in their houses.

When we talk of the Government of India coming in for a Union Territory along with the adjoining State to set up a Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission, what would be the position of Chandigarh? Would you just dictate from here as to what is to be the rate for Chandigarh and as to what is your concept of rationalisation? Or, would you again impress upon the adjoining State of Punjab to form a Joint Commission with the Union Territory, the charge of the Union Territory of Chandigarh being taken by you? I am not clear about this. I would request the hon. Minister to take care of this aspect with the ultimate objective of ensuring that when you talk of rationalisation of electricity tariff you must keep the interests of the residents of Chandigarh in mind.

Of late, we talk of reforms as the mantra of the coming decades. We are still trying to understand what it means. Only yesterday we were told that reforms in labour sector means that you can shunt out labour wherever you wish to. I really fail to understand it. But as far as electricity is concerned, we understand that the generation of electricity in the country is the barometer to gauge the

progress of the country. I do agree and it has to be emphasised that this decides the various other needs for infrastructure. No longer perhaps can we afford to overlook theft or misuse of electricity in one form or the other. I agree with that. That is how perhaps we can quicken our pace in providing electricity to all the villages, particularly to a State like Bihar where according to the present estimates it would take over 700 years to electrify every village in the State. I do find a ray of hope. I only wish the Government matches its words by its deeds since the hon. Minister of Finance yesterday said that they wish to energise all the villages in the next seven years. I wish them well on that front and we would extend all our co-operation thereon. But the point I am trying to make is that in this process and in our anxiety to bring about such reforms we must not ignore the poorest of the poor.

It has become a fashion with us to say that the poor people living in slums are a burden for the society. I wish we gave up this approach. There has got to be an element of cross-subsidisation in all our tariff structures. We can talk of progress and development only if we can ensure that every citizen of the country enjoys the fruits of independence. It is our duty to take care of them.

There are people who can have ten air-conditioners at their places. "Since they can pay at this rate, why should the poor man also not pay at the same rate?", you argue. This would not be fair. People in places like Chandigarh are coming to me and they want to be provided with meters. But we do not make arrangements to provide them with meters. When there is a kundi connection, they raise a hue and cry. Nobody wants to steal electricity and we would not support that. But we would certainly wish that the Government formulates scheme for the poor. There was that Indira Kutir Jyoti Yojana. What has happened to that? There was a commitment of the Government of India to provide at least one light point to every household. What are we doing about that? I ask this only to emphasise the point that when you fix the rates you have got to have an element of cross subsidisation. People who are well off, and people who do not even know what is their electricity bill, if they are made to pay a little more to ensure that this brings light to the dark dwellings of the disadvantaged, I think it would be a very laudatory objective that the Government would serve.

I would request the Minister, while supporting this Bill, to take into account the difficulties which Union Territories like Chandigarh face. They do not have any source of power generation on their own except to draw electricity from else where, but in return serve the adjoining States. Chandigarh is the joint Capital of Punjab and Haryana. Chandigarh has a large number of officials of the Central Government. It has the potential to be developed into a major tourist centre. It is known worldwide for its Rock Garden. It can be developed into a convention centre and can serve as a second place for Delhi where you can spill over your meetings and conventions. With the importance that Chandigarh has today, please do not ignore or overlook the needs of the people of Chandigarh. Take care of its needs.

With these words, I would like to support this Bill.

*m04

turns.label: Ummareddy Venkateswarlu
turns.text:
Sir, I rise to support The Electricity Regulatory Commissions (Amendment) Bill, 1999. At the outset, I must congratulate the hon. Minister for having brought out this Amendment Bill. It is a timely Bill and well thought out Bill to meet the needs of several smaller States whose economic viability is a fundamental issue when we bring certain enactments. Though the original Electricity Regulatory Commission was brought in 1998, some smaller States, like the States in North-Eastern region, have expressed problems that it would be economically very burdensome for the States to meet the expenditure of this Regulatory Commission. Since there is shortage of qualified personnel, talents and funds, the Government of Nagaland sent a proposal to the Ministry of power for the constitution of a Joint Regulatory Commission for the four States, namely, Assam, Mizoram, Manipur and Nagaland. There is a provision in this Bill for setting up Joint State Electricity Regulatory Commission.

Sir, this Bill had been referred to the Standing Committee on Energy. It had been thoroughly discussed and various angles had been taken into consideration. Hon. Minister has also taken a lot of interest on this particular aspect and it has been felt desirable to bring this amendment Bill.

One issue which has been very thoroughly discussed, I was also a Member of the Standing Committee, is that since more than two States are coming together to have this Commission and since there is only one Chairman with three Members including the Chairman, in course of time certain States may not be in a position to represent on the Commission. It is the question of consensus opinion, whether they can be rotated among all the Member-States, as far as its membership is concerned. Even, with regard to the Chairperson, how best it can be rotated; where the headquarters is to be located as also the supplementary and incremental issues that may come from time to time, can be sorted out within the sittings of this particular Commission. So, I do not think there will be any problem on this front because they go by the consensus and also depending upon the accessibility of the headquarters of the Commission or other facilities that are available..It will certainly have the viability just like any other State Regulatory Commission.

While having this Regulatory Commission we wish that most of the States should get bailed out from the financial contingencies which they are passing through. Hitherto, we are experiencing that most of the Electricity Boards are running in losses. There are States which are not in a position to pay the electricity bills that have been drawn from NTPC also. By having this Regulatory Commission as part of the process of reforms, I think such contingencies, such situations should be overcome and the States should become enriched in generation, distribution, transmission and regulating bills, including cross-subsidisation and other things.

With these few words I support the amendment Bill that has been brought by the hon. Minister.

turns.label: MR. CHAIRMAN
turns.text: We all know that 3.30 p.m. is the time for Private Members’ Business. We are almost on the conclusion of the Bill, which is going on at present. I am sure the House will agree not only to complete this Bill but also the next Bill listed in the name of Shri Joshi, as Item No.14.

turns.label: Ramesh Chennithala
turns.text: Sir, this is an important Bill.

turns.label: MR. CHAIRMAN
turns.text: Nobody is being denied to speak. The point is, the House agrees to complete this Bill and the next Bill listed at Sl. No.14, and after that we will take up the Private Members’ Business.

turns.label: SEVERAL HON. MEMBERS
turns.text: Yes, Sir.

turns.label: Ramesh Chennithala
turns.text:
Mr. Chairman, Sir, this Bill is for a limited purpose. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions are there in our country. This piece of legislation has been brought because the small States wanted to have a Joint Regulatory Commission. The proposal came from the Government of Nagaland for having the North-Eastern Electricity Regulatory Commission because they do not have enough funds, expertise, and manpower to constitute their own regulatory authorities.

Sir, at this juncture, I would like to mention one or two very important points. What are the reasons for constituting regulatory commissions? Have these Regulatory Commissions been able to fulfil their objectives? Had they been functioning properly, the Electricity Boards would not have incurred huge losses. The State Electricity Boards are now in a mess. You examine each and every State Electricity Board. The condition of each State Electricity Board is very deplorable and pitiable. They are incurring huge losses.

What is the objective of this Regulatory Commission? It is to rationalise the electricity tariffs, to have transparent policies, subsidies, promotion of efficiency, environmental policies. I would like to know from my esteemed colleague, Shri Suresh Prabhu whether these normal objectives were fulfilled or attended to by these Regulatory Commissions. These are the noble ideals for constituting this Electricity Commissions. Sir, are these Commissions functioning properly? So, it is the high time for the Ministry of Power to examine and evaluate the performance of the Electricity Regulatory Commission. As far as my knowledge goes the Electricity Commissions are not functioning properly. Their performance has not been evaluated for decades and they are not at all performing their duties well. I think that Government should attend to this very seriously. The thing is that the State Regulatory Commissions are also not functioning properly. I am not criticising anybody. So, the overall performance should be evaluated to know whether they are fulfilling their objectives.

Sir, the power generation is the most important thing in our country and every State is starving for power and every State is demanding more power. Sir, you are very well aware of the NTPC triangle. Once upon a time, Kerala was having surplus electricity. We were giving electricity to Tamil Nadu and Karnataka because we have abundance of natural resources. Hydel power was our strength. But today Kerala badly needs power. For all our efforts, the NTPC triangle has been established. The naptha based power generation project came to our State. It was a blessing for us. But unfortunately because of the high price of naptha the State Government have to spend rupee one crore per day to get electricity.

The State is starving like that. The State is incurring an expenditure of Rs.1 crore per day to give electricity to the people at a subsidised rate. Power generation, transmission and distribution are the three processes involved here. Transmission losses are going up and pilferage in distribution is also going up. We should take certain important measures to check all these things. I do not want to take much time of the House. My suggestion is, there should be a total evaluation and the Minister should examine the performance of the Regularity Authorities and the demands of the States which are really in need of power should be looked into sympathetically. More aid should be given to the States which are starving for power.

*m06

turns.text:
सभापति महोदय, मैं सरकार द्वारा प्रस्तुत विद्युत विनियामक आयोग संशोधन विधेयक 1999 का पुरजोर समर्थन करता हूं। जैसा कि बताया गया कि 1998 में विद्युत विनियामक आयोग का गठन किया गया था और जिन विषयों को लेकर इसका गठन किया गया, वह सही था। विद्युत विनियामक आयोग अधिनियम 1998 के पास होने के बाद सैंट्रल विद्युत विनियामक आयोग और बाद में राज्य विनियामक आयोग की स्थापना हुई। गुजरात, मध्य प्रदेश, यू.पी., पश्चिम बंगाल, अरुणाचल प्रदेश, पंजाब, तमिलनाडु, महाराषट्र, दिल्ली, हरियाणा कर्नाटक और राजस्थान आदि राज्यों में इस प्रकार के आयोग की स्थापना हुई लेकिन सिक्किम और उत्तर पूर्व के जो छोटे राज्य थे, उन चार-पांच राज्यों ने मिल कर नागालैंड की तरफ से केन्p सरकार के पास प्रस्ताव रखा कि हमारे पास चूंकि निधि की कमी है, विशेषज्ञ हमारे पास नहीं हैं और प्रति वर्ष इसके लिए जो काारमिक होने चाहिए, वे भी उपलब्ध नहीं हैं, इन कारणों से उन्होंने असमर्थता क्यक्त की। अब तीन-चार राज्य मिल कर आयोग का गठन करना चाहते हैं। 1998 में इस प्रकार का प्रावधान नहीं था इसलिए विद्युत विनियामक आयोग संशोधन विधेयक 1999 लाया गया। इसके द्वारा केन्p और दो-तीन राज्य मिल कर अथवा दो-तीन राज्य अपने आप मिल कर या केन्p शासित प्रदेश और अन्य राज्य मिल कर अपना संयुक्त विनियामक आयोग गठित कर सकते हैं। विद्युत क्यवस्थाओं को संचालित करने, टैरिफ आदि तय करने, सरलीकरण और पारदारशिता बनाए रखने, पर्यावरण को बनाए रखने में और तत्संबंधी विषयों पर निर्णय लेने में अब ये सक्षम होंगे। जैसा सभी माननीय सदस्यों ने इसका समर्थन किया, मैं भी इसका पुरजोर समर्थन करता हूं।

विद्युत विनियामक आयोग कुछ उद्देश्यों को लेकर बनाया गया थ।, दो-ढ़ाई वर्ष का समय हो गया है। आज बहुत युवा, जोशिले, गतिशील क्यक्तित्व के हाथों में इसका भार है। वह इस क्षेत्र में बहुत कुछ करना चाहते हैं। बहन जयवन्ती जी स्वयं बहुत अनुभवी हैं। ये मिल कर विद्युत के क्षेत्र में क्रांतिकारी परिवर्तन लाना चाहते हैं लेकिन मर्ज बढ़ता गया, ज्यों-ज्यों दवा की। कभी एक साथ उत्तरी ग्रिड फेल हो जाता है जिससे पूरी दिल्ली और उत्तर के चार-पांच राज्यों में अंधेरा हो जाता है। इससे पहले कभी ऐसी स्थिति नहीं आई। उड़ीसा, बंगाल और पूर्वी राज्यों में बिजली की बहुलता थी लेकिन अब वहां ट्रांसमिशन के साधन नहीं हैं। राजस्थान में बिजली की कमी है। अगले महीने विनियामक आयोग मूल्य बढ़ाने वाला है। वे मूल्य इतने ज्यादा बढ़ेंगे कि जनता में उसे लेकर अभी से हाहाकार मचा है। वह किसानों की सबसिडी खत्म करके मनमाने fंग से रेट बढ़ा देगा। राजस्थान में अकाल और सूखा पड़ा है। गुजरात में भूकम्प आया है। ऐसी स्थिति में विनियामक आयोग वस्तु स्थिति पर बिना नजर रखे सबको एक लाठी से हंांकना चाहता है।

राज्यों में विनियामक आयोग से कैसे काम चलेगा? एक तरफ राज्य विद्युत बोडर्स हैं जिन पर करोड़ों रुपया उधार है, वे चुका नहीं पा रहे हैं तो दूसरी तरफ उनके पास साधनों का अभाव है, वे मशीनरी नहीं बदल पाते हैं। एक तरफ वे प्लान्स बनाते हैं तो दूसरी तरफ मशीनरी पुरानी हैं। राजस्थान में कोटा के पॉवर स्टेशन का कभी एक यूनिट चालू रहता है तो दूसरा बंद हो जाता है और कभी दूसरा चालू हो जाता है तो पहला बंद हो जाता है। कभी कभी तो दोनों यूनिट खराब हो जाते हैं। परिणामस्वरुप, दूसरे राज्यो से विद्युत लेनी पड़ती है।

सभापति महोदय, आपको जानकर आश्चर्य होगा कि एक तरफ सरकार कहती है कि किसानों को 6-8 घंटे बिजली दी जायेगी लेकिन 2-3 घंटे ही मिल पाती है। कभी बिजली चली भी जाती है, इसका पता नहीं रहता है। रात के अंधेरे में कड़कड़ाती सर्दी में सब आराम से सो रहे होते हैं लेकिन किसान रातभर खेत में रहता है। इसलिये मैं आपके माध्यम से प्रार्थना करना चाहूंगा कि यह विनियामक आयोग देश हित में बिजली का अधिक से अधिक उत्पादन करने के क्षेत्र में उन्नति करने, उसका विस्तार करने, घाटे को कम करने के लिये और मूल्यों को तय करने में बहुत अच्छा सिr हो, ऐसी कामना करता हूं लेकिन किसानों के हित में ग्रामीण विद्युतीकरण के लिये और उन्हें विद्युत पहुंचाने के लिये सरकार को कठोर कदम उठाने चाहिये। इन्हीं शब्दों के साथ मैं पुरजोर इस विधेयक का समर्थन करता हूं।

Title: Discussion on the Electricity Regulatory Commissions (Amendment) Bill, 1999. (Bill passed.)
Type: GOVERNMENT BILLS
Date: 2001-03-02

Start of the debate:

(no name): 14.54 hrs.
MR. SPEAKER: Now, we take up item no. 13. The House has to allot time for discussion on this Bill as the time has not been allotted. Shall we allot one hour?
SOME HON. MEMBERS: Yes.
Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu: विद्युत मंत्री (श्री सुरेश प्रभु): अध्यक्ष महोदय, इस सदन ने रेगुलेटरी कमीशन 1998 को पारित किया था। इसके तहत कानून में ऐसे प्रावधान थे जिससे c® राज्य को रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन करना था। इसके बाद कई राज्यों ने इस तरह के रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन किया। ऐसे कई राज्य हैं जिन्होंने अपने खुद के कानून पारित करके इस इलैक्ट्रसिटी रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन किया है। केन्p सरकार के पास ऐसे कई राज्यों के रिप्रेजेंटेशन्स आये हैं जिसमें कहा गया है कि कई ऐसे छोटे राज्य हैं जिनके लिये रैगुलेटरी कमीशन बनाना आप्रेशनली ज्यादा इफैक्टिव नहीं होगा। इसलिये, इस बात को ध्यान में रखते हुये हमने इस तरह का कानून लाने का निर्णय किया है जिसमें एक से ज्यादा छोटे राज्यों के लिये जाइंट रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन करना संभव होगा। अध्यक्ष महोदय, आपने इस बिल को पहले स्टैंडिंग कमेटी को रैफर किया था और उसने अपनी रिकमैंडेशन्स दे दी हैं जिन्हें इस बिल में सम्मिलित करके इस बिल को सुधार करके सदन में लाये हैं। मेरी सदन से प्रार्थना है कि जिस तरह पहले इस बिल को पारित किया था, उसी तरह इस बिल को भी पारित किया जाये ताकि एक से ज्यादा छोटे राज्यो के लिये यह रैगुलेटरी कमीशन का गठन करना सम्भव हो सके। अध्यक्ष महोदय, मैं प्रस्ताव करता हूं:
SHRI V.P. SINGH BADNORE (BHILWARA): Sir, I rise to support the proposed Bill amending the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and the States’ Electricity Regulatory Commissions. The Electricity Regulatory Commission Bill became an Act in 1998. This Bill has a very limited role. In the Bill, there was no consideration for small States, which cannot afford to have a State Electricity Regulatory Commission because the Electricity Regulatory Commission in every State must have a lot of other things, like a building, a Commission and other paraphernalia, which is very difficult for a small State to spend so much money on it. The North-Eastern States especially do not want to spend so much money on this. That is why, this Bill is being mooted, and I support it wholeheartedly. I think, this is also an opportunity for us to look into the working of the CERC and the SERCs. This Bill is okay. There may be small problems in this Bill, like if the five North-Eastern States want to have a common State Electricity Regulatory Commission, then who is going to be its Chairman and so on. Alternately, one of the members will have to be its Chairman. It can create some problems; it can also create small problems, like where this State Electricity Regulatory Commission is going to be housed, in which State it is going to be housed and so on. They have to decide this. If they can decide it very amiably, I think, nobody will have any problems about it. It also has only three members in it. Now, if five States are going to have three members, then they may have some problems in deciding who is going to be the member, and who is not going to be the member. This has been left to them, and they are going to sort it out through a consensus. However, I look at it on a bigger scenario. Sir, this is the first Bill being piloted by our new Minister of Power, Shri Suresh Prabhu. I feel that he has a big problem to sort out a lot of other issues. 15.00 hrs. Power is the biggest problem area in this country. Nothing moves without power. Though Shri Yashwant Sinha has presented a very good Budget, yet if there is no power and if there is a shortfall in power and energy, then nothing will move ahead. The IT industry would not move ahead and the other industries also would not move ahead. We would not be able to do any developmental work without power. Sir, but I would like to congratulate the hon. Minister in a way. He has been really working hard on it. It has come to our notice from the reports of the newspapers that the hon. Minister has been trying to understand the problems of this nature. There are many problems that plague the power sector. The biggest of them is that, though the public sector units like the NTPC and NHPC have been performing well, the private sector participation in this sector has not been up to the expectations. There has been a shortfall only because the private sector has not come into this sector the way it should have. Sir, I would not like to go into the long history as to why it has not been happening. I would also not like to go into securitisation and counter-guarantees and such other things. It is because the scope of this Bill is very limited. I would only like to talk about the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and what it has achieved during the last two and a half years. This Commission came into being in the year 1998. What we must see here is this. Has this Commission really taken off? Has it really performed? Why was this Commission set up? Why should we at all have this Commission? Is it doing its work? These are the questions on which we have to ponder over today. 15.02 hrs. (Shri P.H.Pandiyan in the Chair) Sir, the few orders that this Commission has passed have been challenged in the Courts. They had come out with an Order regarding `availability based tariff’. I would like to talk on this subject today. This order of `availability based tariff’ has been challenged by NTPC and this would be challenged in the future also. What exactly is this `availability based tariff’ for the NTPC? The order basically seeks to increase the benchmark level on availability for generating companies from the earlier established level of 68.49 plant load factor to 80 per cent. Sir, earlier there were some problems with TRAI in this regard. That is why, in this Act of the Regulatory Commission, there was a provision saying that the Ministry would be involved and would also be able to give directions to the Regulatory Commission so that the repetition of the problems that TRAI faced would not be there in the field of electricity as well. I feel that the Ministry has not been concerned over this. If the Ministry has been concerned, they would have seen that orders like these are not passed. Why should an order be passed against NTPC? Tomorrow it may be passed against the NHPC also. Those are the performing public sector units and the surplus money that they are making is being ploughed back for augmentation of the power industry only. I would request that this be looked into. I feel that some sort of directions from the Ministry must go to the CERC regarding passing of such orders. One of the reasons why the Regulatory Commissions came into being was that we wanted to have an independent body to look into the tariff structure. The SEBs have all failed today. They are all in the red because the States have not been able to pay to SEBs. If SEBs are not performing well, and if they continue to be in the red, there is going to be more problems in this industry. To look into this whole affair CERC and SERCs have been set up. I would like to know if any orders of SERCs have really gone into the tariff realisation so far. If they have failed to do this, who is going to pay this subsidy amount? This particular Bill is a very small Bill and in this context I am talking. I would say in the bigger context that CERC and SERCs have not really performed. This is what the Minister must explain to us. With these words, I support this Bill.
Pawan Kumar Bansal: Mr. Chairman, Sir, this Bill has ostensibly been moved to meet the need and demand of smaller States to enable them to set up Joint Electricity Regulatory Commissions. This is a welcome measure. By the way the ‘Statement of Objects and Reasons’ of the Bill has been wrongly printed as ‘Statement of Objections and Reasons’.
Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu: Your objection is sustained, Sir.
Pawan Kumar Bansal: Thank you. That was just by the way. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill refers to the communication that the Government of India had received from the Government of Nagaland for constitution of a joint North-Eastern Electricity Regulatory Commission for four States – Assam, Mizoram, Manipur and Nagaland. Besides Nagaland, we are told that Sikkim and other North-Eastern States have also indicated their problems in setting up individual Commissions due to factors like paucity of funds, personnel, talent, etc. Therefore, this Bill becomes the need of the hour, if we really wish to subserve the objective of the main legislation. Besides that, I also think that via this Bill, we could set the pace for cooperation between different States. Today, we find that the borders of the States tend to become borders of contention, I suppose, cooperation between the States in setting up of joint bodies on matters beginning with the Electricity Regulatory Commission would serve a very useful purpose, and such borders would, in fact, become places where the citizens of one State are out to meet with a smile their friends from the other States. Sir, having said that, I would like to seize this opportunity to refer to the peculiar problem of the place I come from. We talk of small States. I come from a small Union Territory. Unfortunately, the need of the Union Territory of Chandigarh has not been taken care of the way it should have been. Many years back, we were assured of a generation plant there at Chandigarh itself. We are now told that it would not be viable and it would be a difficult proposition. Though I would wish that we have one, but I do not intend to dispute the assessment of the Government in this regard. But, Sir, what I would really like to point out is that, for not years but for decades, we have been raising a demand for according us our due in the form of membership of Bhakra Beas Management Board. That is our legitimate right even according to the provisions of the Punjab Reorganisation Act. But somehow, it is Punjab and Haryana perhaps, the two States which have adopted a big-brotherly attitude and resisted the membership of Chandigarh to the Bhakra Beas Management Board. Despite the fact that Chandigarh has an excellent record of distribution and even resource generation on many counts, while States like Punjab -- as we have seen in the past -- have been squandering away their resources on the populous measures, yet Chandigarh has to suffer for no fault of its own. Whenever the question of fixation of tariff arises, we are told, "Well, these are the rates prevailing in the adjoining State of Punjab. Therefore, Chandigarh must have the same rate." There is no rationale behind that. But we, people of Chandigarh, are helpless. We do not have a representative body like the Legislative Assembly where the aspirations, yearnings and the needs of the people could be articulated. We have to content with what is decided by the Government of India here and finally implemented through its officers at Chandigarh. Sir, if the membership of BBMB is accorded to Chandigarh, Chandigarh would draw power at lesser rate.
MR. CHAIRMAN: Since, there is no panel of Chairmen present here, and as I have to join the Business Advisory Committee meeting in hon. Speaker’s Chamber, if the House agrees, I would request Shri G.M. Banatwalla to occupy the Chair.
SOME HON. MEMBERS: Sure, Sir. 15.14 hrs (Shri G.M. Banatwalla in the Chair )
Pawan Kumar Bansal: Mr. Chairman, Sir, if Chandigarh is accorded membership of Bhakra Beas Management Board, the rate at which electricity would be provided to Chandigarh would come down, with the result, people would get electricity at cheaper rate. You leave it to the Administration that it must not incur losses thereon. That is fine. But the people must not be taxed for no fault of theirs, rather, they should not be deprived of their right which is there. In the past, we have seen that whenever the tariff of electricity in the Union Territory has been enhanced thoughtlessly, there is always a steep hike even in the minimum charges fixed. I can understand the concept of fixation of minimum charges for industry and for commercial sector. To have minimum charges for domestic consumers and that too at an abnormally high rate is beyond imagination and without rationale. Chandigarh is a place where people have houses of an acre or even more than an acre.
Nitish Sengupta: But do not pay the house tax.
Pawan Kumar Bansal: I will deal with the question as to why the people of Chandigarh would not pay that separately. It is because they were coaxed to come to Chandigarh. Perhaps the hon. Member is not aware of the circumstances in which the city of Chandigarh was raised. Pandit Nehru took interest in it; Sardar Pratap Singh Kairon took interest in it. They in fact promised much more than what the people there are getting today to go and settle in Chandigarh. That is how this city was then raised. I was referring to the abnormal increase in the rates of minimum charges. People living in big houses are generally retired people. There are just two retired elderly people in those houses – the husband and the wife – with their children settled in other places. On the one hand, we exhort people to save electricity. Maybe the sanctioned load for those houses is much bigger but going by the advice of the Government and going by the need of the society to save electricity, they would switch off the light when they go out and switch on the fan when they come back. That way, they save electricity wherever possible. But they often find that the charges that are slapped on them are much more than what they have actually consumed. Is that fair in such cases? I would take this opportunity to impress upon the hon. Minister to ensure that as far as the domestic consumers are concerned such burden should not be imposed on them and the bills should be just according to the actual consumption of the residents in their houses. When we talk of the Government of India coming in for a Union Territory along with the adjoining State to set up a Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission, what would be the position of Chandigarh? Would you just dictate from here as to what is to be the rate for Chandigarh and as to what is your concept of rationalisation? Or, would you again impress upon the adjoining State of Punjab to form a Joint Commission with the Union Territory, the charge of the Union Territory of Chandigarh being taken by you? I am not clear about this. I would request the hon. Minister to take care of this aspect with the ultimate objective of ensuring that when you talk of rationalisation of electricity tariff you must keep the interests of the residents of Chandigarh in mind. Of late, we talk of reforms as the mantra of the coming decades. We are still trying to understand what it means. Only yesterday we were told that reforms in labour sector means that you can shunt out labour wherever you wish to. I really fail to understand it. But as far as electricity is concerned, we understand that the generation of electricity in the country is the barometer to gauge the progress of the country. I do agree and it has to be emphasised that this decides the various other needs for infrastructure. No longer perhaps can we afford to overlook theft or misuse of electricity in one form or the other. I agree with that. That is how perhaps we can quicken our pace in providing electricity to all the villages, particularly to a State like Bihar where according to the present estimates it would take over 700 years to electrify every village in the State. I do find a ray of hope. I only wish the Government matches its words by its deeds since the hon. Minister of Finance yesterday said that they wish to energise all the villages in the next seven years. I wish them well on that front and we would extend all our co-operation thereon. But the point I am trying to make is that in this process and in our anxiety to bring about such reforms we must not ignore the poorest of the poor. It has become a fashion with us to say that the poor people living in slums are a burden for the society. I wish we gave up this approach. There has got to be an element of cross-subsidisation in all our tariff structures. We can talk of progress and development only if we can ensure that every citizen of the country enjoys the fruits of independence. It is our duty to take care of them. There are people who can have ten air-conditioners at their places. "Since they can pay at this rate, why should the poor man also not pay at the same rate?", you argue. This would not be fair. People in places like Chandigarh are coming to me and they want to be provided with meters. But we do not make arrangements to provide them with meters. When there is a kundi connection, they raise a hue and cry. Nobody wants to steal electricity and we would not support that. But we would certainly wish that the Government formulates scheme for the poor. There was that Indira Kutir Jyoti Yojana. What has happened to that? There was a commitment of the Government of India to provide at least one light point to every household. What are we doing about that? I ask this only to emphasise the point that when you fix the rates you have got to have an element of cross subsidisation. People who are well off, and people who do not even know what is their electricity bill, if they are made to pay a little more to ensure that this brings light to the dark dwellings of the disadvantaged, I think it would be a very laudatory objective that the Government would serve. I would request the Minister, while supporting this Bill, to take into account the difficulties which Union Territories like Chandigarh face. They do not have any source of power generation on their own except to draw electricity from else where, but in return serve the adjoining States. Chandigarh is the joint Capital of Punjab and Haryana. Chandigarh has a large number of officials of the Central Government. It has the potential to be developed into a major tourist centre. It is known worldwide for its Rock Garden. It can be developed into a convention centre and can serve as a second place for Delhi where you can spill over your meetings and conventions. With the importance that Chandigarh has today, please do not ignore or overlook the needs of the people of Chandigarh. Take care of its needs. With these words, I would like to support this Bill. *m04
